title: Six National Monuments Targeted for Mining and Drilling
description_short: Six National Monuments Targeted for Mining and Drilling
description_medium: In February 2025, Interior Secretary Burgum ordered a review of all national monuments for potential boundary reductions to enable energy and mining development. By April 2025, Interior aides were actively analyzing geological maps to assess six monuments for shrinkage: Bears Ears and Grand Staircase-Escalante in Utah, Baaj Nwaavjo I'tah Kukveni-Ancestral Footprints of the Grand Canyon and Ironwood Forest in Arizona, Organ Mountains-Desert Peaks in New Mexico, and Chuckwalla in California. Grand Staircase-Escalante holds large coal reserves; Bears Ears contains uranium deposits.
description_long:
In February 2025, Interior Secretary Burgum ordered a review of all national monuments for potential boundary reductions to enable energy and mining development. By April 2025, Interior aides were actively analyzing geological maps to assess six monuments for shrinkage: Bears Ears and Grand Staircase-Escalante in Utah, Baaj Nwaavjo I'tah Kukveni-Ancestral Footprints of the Grand Canyon and Ironwood Forest in Arizona, Organ Mountains-Desert Peaks in New Mexico, and Chuckwalla in California. Grand Staircase-Escalante holds large coal reserves; Bears Ears contains uranium deposits. The monuments collectively protect millions of acres of Indigenous sacred land and unique ecosystems.

The review and analysis described here are preparatory steps, distinct from completed changes to monument boundaries or permission for a particular mine. The list of six sites identifies where officials were considering action, while the mineral references help explain the development interest. These lands have conservation and cultural significance in addition to resource potential. The supplied account does not establish that every proposal proceeded, or quantify damage resulting from development, so those outcomes should not be inferred.

title: Trump Bedminster Golf Club: Secret Service Pays $540K Between 2017-2020
description_short: Trump Bedminster Golf Club: Secret Service Pays $540K Between 2017-2020
description_medium: At Trump National Golf Club in Bedminster, New Jersey alone, the Secret Service paid approximately $540,000 over the course of Trump's first term for accommodations and facilities needed to protect the president during his frequent visits. The payments went directly to a Trump-owned entity, enriching the president while he was in office. Congressional Democrats repeatedly demanded accounting of all such payments across all Trump properties. The Bedminster figure was just one piece of a much larger pattern of taxpayer money flowing to Trump's personal golf empire.
description_long:
At Trump National Golf Club in Bedminster, New Jersey alone, the Secret Service paid approximately $540,000 over the course of Trump's first term for accommodations and facilities needed to protect the president during his frequent visits. The payments went directly to a Trump-owned entity, enriching the president while he was in office. Congressional Democrats repeatedly demanded accounting of all such payments across all Trump properties. The Bedminster figure was just one piece of a much larger pattern of taxpayer money flowing to Trump's personal golf empire. No independent audit was ever completed during his presidency.

Protection of a president requires accommodations for agents, but using a president-owned property makes the choice of venue financially consequential for that president's business. The reported Bedminster payments identify one location and one period, not the entire cost of presidential security. Congressional requests for accounting addressed the broader need to trace those payments. The figure should be read as spending on accommodations and facilities, rather than the president's net personal profit after expenses.

title: Power Plant Greenhouse Gas Rules Repealed, Coal Plants Unleashed
description_short: Power Plant Greenhouse Gas Rules Repealed, Coal Plants Unleashed
description_medium: On June 11, 2025, the EPA proposed repealing Biden-era rules limiting greenhouse gas emissions from coal and natural gas power plants, framing the rollback as saving industry 'billions of dollars.' The agency simultaneously proposed weakening mercury emission standards for power plants, pollutants linked to brain damage in children and cardiovascular disease in adults. EPA Administrator Zeldin claimed the regulations were inconsistent with the Clean Air Act.
description_long:
On June 11, 2025, the EPA proposed repealing Biden-era rules limiting greenhouse gas emissions from coal and natural gas power plants, framing the rollback as saving industry 'billions of dollars.' The agency simultaneously proposed weakening mercury emission standards for power plants, pollutants linked to brain damage in children and cardiovascular disease in adults. EPA Administrator Zeldin claimed the regulations were inconsistent with the Clean Air Act. Environmental groups warned the repeal would set back decades of progress on air quality and dramatically increase climate-warming emissions from the electricity sector, one of the US's largest emissions sources.

The announcement concerned proposed repeals. Its projected savings depended on finalization, so it did not itself establish that the standards had already disappeared or that industry costs had already fallen. Greenhouse-gas limits and mercury standards address different pollutants, even though both proposals concern the electricity sector. Zeldin's statutory argument and environmental organizations' warnings describe opposing assessments of the policy. The record documents the regulatory initiative without treating projected health or emissions effects as completed outcomes.

title: DNI Gabbard Releases Documents on Russia Investigation Whistleblower (July 2025)
description_short: DNI Gabbard Releases Documents on Russia Investigation Whistleblower (July 2025)
description_medium: On July 30, 2025, Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard released new documents providing a firsthand account of a senior intelligence official's efforts to expose what she described as manipulated intelligence behind the Russia-collusion narrative, including work in the months before the November 2016 election and pressure regarding the January 2017 Intelligence Community Assessment (ODNI News Release No. 19-25). Reuters reported on the release and a DOJ response in July 2025.
description_long:
On July 30, 2025, Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard released new documents providing a firsthand account of a senior intelligence official's efforts to expose what she described as manipulated intelligence behind the Russia-collusion narrative, including work in the months before the November 2016 election and pressure regarding the January 2017 Intelligence Community Assessment (ODNI News Release No. 19-25). Reuters reported on the release and a DOJ response in July 2025. The card's March 2025 date and its claim of a release simultaneously covering COVID origins, the Russia investigation, and the 2020 election are not supported.

The release is evidence of what Gabbard publicly asserted and the material she chose to disclose. It is not, by its issuance alone, proof of the underlying allegation that intelligence was manipulated. The corrected account locates the documents in the 2016–2017 intelligence dispute and preserves attribution to the director. That focus avoids combining unrelated COVID-origin and 2020-election issues, while leaving the merits of the allegations distinct from the fact and date of the disclosure.

title: Trump Threatens North Korea with 'Fire and Fury'
description_short: Trump Threatens North Korea with 'Fire and Fury'
description_medium: Amid escalating tensions over North Korea's nuclear weapons testing, President Trump delivered an impromptu and bellicose threat on August 8, 2017, stating that further threats to the US would be met with 'fire and fury like the world has never seen.' The inflammatory rhetoric, delivered off-the-cuff from his golf club in New Jersey, shocked allies and defense experts who feared it could inadvertently trigger a nuclear conflict.
description_long:
Amid escalating tensions over North Korea's nuclear weapons testing, President Trump delivered an impromptu and bellicose threat on August 8, 2017, stating that further threats to the US would be met with 'fire and fury like the world has never seen.' The inflammatory rhetoric, delivered off-the-cuff from his golf club in New Jersey, shocked allies and defense experts who feared it could inadvertently trigger a nuclear conflict. The administration engaged in months of brinkmanship, with Trump frequently taunting leader Kim Jong-un as 'Little Rocket Man' before eventually pivoting to holding historic, yet largely fruitless, summits with the dictator.

The statement was a public threat made during an exchange of warnings, rather than an announcement that the United States had begun a nuclear attack. Its significance lay in the escalation risk identified by observers and the uncertainty about how the North Korean government would respond. The later turn toward meetings with Kim was a different phase of the relationship. Keeping those phases distinct allows an account of threatening rhetoric without suggesting the warning itself caused a war.
